# LLM APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Open Models) ##### The key that cost ₹6.4 lakh in eleven hours A student in Bhopal built a study assistant over a weekend, pushed it to a public GitHub repository, and went to sleep pleased with himself. His `app.py` contained this line: ```python client = OpenAI(api_key="sk-proj-...") ``` Automated scrapers monitor GitHub for API key patterns. His key was found in under four minutes. By morning it had made roughly 180,000 requests to GPT-4 from IP addresses across three continents. The bill was ₹6,41,000. OpenAI waived it — they usually do for a first, obvious compromise — but the account was suspended for two weeks and the incident is permanent in his memory. **Never put a key in your source code.** Not temporarily, not "just for testing," not in a private repo you plan to make public later. Today starts there, because everything else in this article is worthless if you leak the credential. ##### Environment variables and secrets ```bash # .env — NEVER commit this OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-proj-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx ``` ```bash # .gitignore .env .env.* *.key ``` ```python import os from dotenv import load_dotenv load_dotenv() api_key = os.environ.get("OPENAI_API_KEY") if not api_key: raise RuntimeError("OPENAI_API_KEY is not set. Copy .env.example to .env.") ``` Commit a `.env.example` with the variable names and empty values, so collaborators know what to set. In production use your platform's secret manager — AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, or the hosting provider's environment settings — never a file on disk. Two more habits worth building now: **set a monthly spend limit** in the provider dashboard before your first call, and **rotate keys** if there is any doubt. Both take under a minute. ##### Chat completions Every modern LLM API uses the same message-list shape you saw on Day 30. ```python from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI() # reads OPENAI_API_KEY from the environment response = client.chat.completions.create( model="gpt-4o-mini", messages=[ {"role": "system", "content": "You are a concise logistics assistant for an Indian company. " "Answer in 3 sentences maximum."}, {"role": "user", "content": "What documents are needed for interstate GST transport?"}, ], temperature=0.3, max_tokens=300, ) print(response.choices[0].message.content) print(f"tokens: {response.usage.prompt_tokens} in, " f"{response.usage.completion_tokens} out") print("finish reason:", response.choices[0].finish_reason) ``` **Always check `finish_reason`.** `"stop"` means the model finished naturally. `"length"` means it hit `max_tokens` and got cut off mid-sentence — a silent failure that produces truncated output your users will notice before you do. Anthropic's SDK is structurally similar with one notable difference — the system prompt is a top-level parameter, not a message: ```python from anthropic import Anthropic client = Anthropic() message = client.messages.create( model="claude-3-5-haiku-20241022", max_tokens=300, # required, not optional system="You are a concise logistics assistant.", # top-level messages=[ {"role": "user", "content": "What documents are needed for interstate GST transport?"}, ], temperature=0.3, ) print(message.content[0].text) print(f"tokens: {message.usage.input_tokens} in, {message.usage.output_tokens} out") ``` **Open models** are served through OpenAI-compatible endpoints by most providers, so the same client works: ```python # Local via Ollama client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:11434/v1", api_key="ollama") # Together, Groq, Fireworks, vLLM — all expose /v1/chat/completions client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.groq.com/openai/v1", api_key=os.environ["GROQ_API_KEY"]) ``` That compatibility is deliberate and useful: **write against the OpenAI interface and you can switch providers with one line.** For Indian startups, self-hosting a Llama or Mistral model on a rented GPU often beats per-token pricing once volume is steady. ##### Temperature and top-p From Day 24, now with practical guidance: | Task | Temperature | top_p | |---|---|---| | Extraction, classification, JSON | **0.0** | 1.0 | | Factual Q&A, RAG answers | 0.0–0.3 | 1.0 | | General conversation | 0.5–0.7 | 0.95 | | Creative writing, brainstorming | 0.8–1.1 | 0.95 | **Change one, not both.** Temperature reshapes the distribution; top-p truncates it. Adjusting both simultaneously makes the effect hard to reason about, and the standard advice from both OpenAI and Anthropic is to fix one at its default. A caution: even at `temperature=0`, outputs are not perfectly deterministic across calls, due to floating-point non-determinism in batched GPU inference. It is *nearly* deterministic, which is enough for production but not enough to build exact-match tests on. Other parameters worth knowing: ```python response = client.chat.completions.create( model="gpt-4o-mini", messages=messages, temperature=0.0, max_tokens=500, stop=["\n\n###", "END"], # stop generation at these strings seed=42, # best-effort reproducibility frequency_penalty=0.0, # reduce token repetition presence_penalty=0.0, # encourage new topics ) ``` ##### Streaming A three-second wait feels broken. The same three seconds with text appearing token by token feels fast. Streaming is a UX decision more than a technical one, and it is why every chat interface uses it. ```python def stream_response(client, messages, model="gpt-4o-mini", **kwargs): """Yield content chunks as they arrive.""" stream = client.chat.completions.create( model=model, messages=messages, stream=True, stream_options={"include_usage": True}, # get token counts at the end **kwargs, ) usage = None for chunk in stream: if chunk.usage: usage = chunk.usage if chunk.choices and chunk.choices[0].delta.content: yield chunk.choices[0].delta.content if usage: yield f"\n\n[{usage.prompt_tokens} in / {usage.completion_tokens} out]" for piece in stream_response(client, messages): print(piece, end="", flush=True) ``` `flush=True` matters — without it Python buffers stdout and you get the whole response at once anyway, defeating the point. **The trade-offs of streaming:** you cannot validate the complete output before showing it to the user, so JSON mode and structured output are awkward to combine with it. And token usage only arrives at the end, which is why `stream_options={"include_usage": True}` exists. Anthropic's streaming API is similar: ```python with client.messages.stream(model="claude-3-5-haiku-20241022", max_tokens=500, messages=messages) as stream: for text in stream.text_stream: print(text, end="", flush=True) final = stream.get_final_message() ``` ##### Structured output Day 30 covered prompting for JSON. The APIs now offer something stronger: **constrained decoding**, where invalid output is impossible rather than merely unlikely. ```python from pydantic import BaseModel, Field from typing import Literal class TicketAnalysis(BaseModel): category: Literal["billing", "technical", "delivery", "account", "other"] urgency: Literal["low", "medium", "high"] summary: str = Field(..., max_length=200) requires_human: bool suggested_action: str completion = client.beta.chat.completions.parse( model="gpt-4o-mini", messages=[ {"role": "system", "content": "Analyse the support ticket."}, {"role": "user", "content": "My UPI payment was debited twice for order #4471 " "and nobody has replied in 3 days."}, ], response_format=TicketAnalysis, temperature=0.0, ) result = completion.choices[0].message.parsed print(result.category, result.urgency, result.requires_human) ``` The `parsed` field is a validated Pydantic object. The model *cannot* return a category outside the `Literal` set, because the decoder is constrained to the schema. The older JSON mode is still widely available and works with any provider: ```python response = client.chat.completions.create( model="gpt-4o-mini", messages=[{"role": "system", "content": "Respond only in JSON."}, ...], response_format={"type": "json_object"}, # guarantees valid JSON, not a schema temperature=0.0, ) data = json.loads(response.choices[0].message.content) ``` Note the difference: `json_object` guarantees *parseable* JSON; `json_schema`/Pydantic guarantees JSON *matching your schema*. Use the latter where available. ##### Error handling and retries This is what separates a demo from something you can run in production. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["API call"] --> B{"Response?"} B -->|200 OK| C["Return result"] B -->|429 Rate limit| D["Exponential backoff
+ jitter, retry"] B -->|500/502/503| D B -->|Timeout| D B -->|401 Auth| E["FAIL FAST
key is wrong"] B -->|400 Bad request| F["FAIL FAST
fix the request"] B -->|context_length_exceeded| G["Truncate input, retry once"] D --> H{"Attempts
exhausted?"} H -->|No| A H -->|Yes| I["Raise / fall back
to smaller model"] ``` ```python import time import random import logging from openai import OpenAI, RateLimitError, APITimeoutError, APIStatusError, APIError logger = logging.getLogger(__name__) client = OpenAI(timeout=30.0, max_retries=0) # we handle retries ourselves RETRYABLE = (RateLimitError, APITimeoutError) def call_llm(messages, model="gpt-4o-mini", max_attempts=5, **kwargs): """Call an LLM with exponential backoff and jitter.""" for attempt in range(max_attempts): try: response = client.chat.completions.create( model=model, messages=messages, **kwargs ) if response.choices[0].finish_reason == "length": logger.warning("Response truncated by max_tokens") return response except RETRYABLE as exc: if attempt == max_attempts - 1: logger.error("Exhausted retries: %s", exc) raise # Exponential backoff with full jitter delay = min(60, (2 ** attempt)) * (0.5 + random.random()) logger.warning("Attempt %d failed (%s); retrying in %.1fs", attempt + 1, type(exc).__name__, delay) time.sleep(delay) except APIStatusError as exc: if exc.status_code >= 500: # server error — retryable delay = min(60, 2 ** attempt) * (0.5 + random.random()) time.sleep(delay) continue logger.error("Non-retryable %d: %s", exc.status_code, exc) raise # 400, 401, 403 — fail fast ``` **Jitter is the detail people skip.** Without random jitter, every client that hit a rate limit retries at exactly the same moment, producing a synchronised thundering herd that triggers the limit again. Adding `(0.5 + random.random())` spreads them out. **Fail fast on 4xx errors** other than 429. Retrying a malformed request or a bad API key five times just wastes thirty seconds before failing anyway. ##### Cost tracking ```python # ₹ per 1,000 tokens (illustrative — check current pricing) PRICING = { "gpt-4o-mini": {"in": 0.0125, "out": 0.050}, "gpt-4o": {"in": 0.21, "out": 0.84}, "claude-3-5-haiku": {"in": 0.067, "out": 0.33}, "claude-3-5-sonnet": {"in": 0.25, "out": 1.25}, } class CostTracker: def __init__(self): self.calls = 0 self.tokens_in = 0 self.tokens_out = 0 self.cost = 0.0 def record(self, model, usage): p = PRICING.get(model) if not p: return self.calls += 1 self.tokens_in += usage.prompt_tokens self.tokens_out += usage.completion_tokens self.cost += (usage.prompt_tokens / 1000) * p["in"] self.cost += (usage.completion_tokens / 1000) * p["out"] def report(self): return (f"{self.calls} calls | {self.tokens_in:,} in / " f"{self.tokens_out:,} out | ₹{self.cost:.2f}") ``` **Cost-reduction levers, roughly in order of impact:** 1. **Use a smaller model.** `gpt-4o-mini` is often 15–20× cheaper than `gpt-4o` and adequate for classification, extraction, and routing. 2. **Shorten prompts.** Every call pays for the full system prompt. Trim ruthlessly. 3. **Cap `max_tokens`.** Output tokens cost 3–5× input tokens. 4. **Cache repeated calls.** An LRU cache on identical prompts is free money. 5. **Use prompt caching** where the provider offers it — a long fixed preamble can be cached at a fraction of the price. 6. **Batch APIs** offer around 50% discounts for non-urgent work. ##### Conversation memory Chat APIs are **stateless**. The model remembers nothing between calls; you resend the history every time. ```python class Conversation: def __init__(self, system_prompt, max_turns=10): self.system = {"role": "system", "content": system_prompt} self.history = [] self.max_turns = max_turns def add(self, role, content): self.history.append({"role": role, "content": content}) # Keep the last N exchanges; the system prompt always stays if len(self.history) > self.max_turns * 2: self.history = self.history[-self.max_turns * 2:] @property def messages(self): return [self.system] + self.history ``` That truncation matters because **you pay for the entire history on every turn.** A 30-turn conversation resends 30 turns of context each time, so cost grows quadratically. Real systems truncate, summarise older turns, or both. ##### Common mistakes - **Hardcoding API keys** — the ₹6.4 lakh mistake. - **No spend limit** configured in the dashboard. - **Ignoring `finish_reason`**, shipping silently truncated responses. - **Retrying 4xx errors** that will never succeed. - **No jitter** in backoff, causing synchronised retry storms. - **Adjusting temperature and top_p together.** - **Forgetting the API is stateless** and expecting it to remember. - **Unbounded conversation history**, growing cost and eventually blowing the context window. - **No timeout**, so a hung request blocks your worker indefinitely. - **Not logging token usage**, making cost debugging impossible. - **Using the largest model by default** instead of testing whether a small one suffices. - **Sending PII to a third-party API** without checking data retention terms — relevant under the DPDP Act 2023. ##### Hands-on: build the client layer properly Your practical task is a script that calls an LLM with a system prompt, streams the response, and returns structured JSON. These pull in opposite directions — streaming shows partial output, structured output needs the whole thing — so make a deliberate choice: stream a human-readable answer, then make a second non-streaming call for the structured extraction. Recognising that tension is the actual lesson. The mini project is a CLI chatbot with memory, streaming, and cost tracking. Print the running cost after every turn. Watching `₹0.04 → ₹0.11 → ₹0.23 → ₹0.41` climb as the conversation grows makes the quadratic cost of resending history viscerally obvious in a way no explanation does. Add a `/cost` and `/clear` command; you will want both. The assignment implements robust error handling with retries and rate-limit backoff. Test it properly rather than hoping: use a deliberately invalid model name to trigger a 400 and confirm it fails fast, and use a monkeypatched client that raises `RateLimitError` twice then succeeds, to confirm the backoff path works. Document which errors you retry and why — that reasoning is what an interviewer probes. ##### Key takeaways - **Never hardcode API keys.** Use environment variables, gitignore your `.env`, and set a spend limit before your first call. - **The chat completions shape is near-universal** — write against the OpenAI interface and you can switch to Anthropic, Groq, or a self-hosted model with minimal change. - **Stream for UX, use `temperature=0` and constrained structured output for correctness**, and always check `finish_reason` for silent truncation. - **Retry 429s and 5xx with exponential backoff plus jitter; fail fast on 400s and 401s** — and jitter is what prevents synchronised retry storms. - **The API is stateless and you pay for the full history every turn**, so track cost per call, truncate conversations, and default to the smallest model that does the job.
